definitions.answer:
These are the metrics the evaluations record, grouped by the kind of task they apply to. A metric appears on a result only when that evaluation recorded it.

Forecasting and regression
- Mean absolute error (MAE): The average size of the miss, ignoring direction: on a typical day the forecast is off by about this much. Lower is better. Unit: target_units. Keep in mind: Depends on the scale of what is forecast, so it cannot be compared across different targets.
- Root mean squared error (RMSE): Like MAE but large misses count more, so it rises when a few forecasts are far off. Lower is better. Unit: target_units. Keep in mind: Always at least as large as MAE; the gap between the two shows how uneven the errors are.
- Weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE): Total absolute error divided by total actual volume: the share of volume that was mis-forecast. Lower is better. Unit: percent. Keep in mind: Dominated by the high-volume days when demand is intermittent. Not defined when the actual total is zero.
- Bias (mean error) (Bias): The average signed error (forecast minus actual). It shows whether the forecast leans high or low. Closer to zero is better. Unit: target_units. Positive = over-forecast (forecast above actual). Negative = under-forecast. Keep in mind: Over- and under-forecasts cancel, so a bias near zero does not mean the forecasts are accurate.
- Relative bias (Rel. bias): Signed error as a share of total actual volume. Closer to zero is better. Unit: percent. Positive = over-forecast. Negative = under-forecast. Keep in mind: Not defined when the actual total is zero.
- Mean absolute percentage error (MAPE): The average miss as a percentage of the actual value on each day. Lower is better. Unit: percent. Keep in mind: Unreliable whenever some actual values are zero or very small: one near-zero day can dominate the whole figure. Prefer WAPE.
- Prediction-interval coverage (Coverage): The share of held-out actual values that fell inside the forecast's uncertainty band. Closer to the promised level is better. Unit: percent. Keep in mind: Compare with the level the band promises (for example 80%). Held-out points overlap in time, so this is an approximate check.
- Baseline MAE (yesterday's value) (Baseline MAE): The MAE of the simplest forecast: repeat the previous day's value, measured on the same rows and period as the model. Lower is better. Unit: target_units. Keep in mind: A model is only useful if it beats this.
- Change in MAE vs baseline (vs baseline): How much lower (positive) or higher (negative) the model's MAE is than the baseline's on the same rows. Higher is better. Unit: percent. Keep in mind: Computed from two recorded MAE values; it is not a new measurement.
- Root mean squared scaled error (RMSSE): Each series' RMSE divided by the RMSE of the simple one-step 'repeat yesterday' forecast on that series' own training history, then averaged over series. Below 1 means the forecasts are better than that simple rule would have been; above 1 means worse. Lower is better. Unit: ratio. Keep in mind: Unit-free, so it suits many series of different sizes. Series whose training history never changed cannot be scaled and are left out (their number is shown). Only comparable between rows of the same benchmark run.
- Aggregate-day WAPE (Agg. WAPE): WAPE after adding all series together for each day: how far off the forecast total is for the whole range on a typical day. Lower is better. Unit: percent. Keep in mind: Errors in different series cancel when added up, so this is far lower than the per-series WAPE and must not be compared with it.
- Median series WAPE (Median WAPE): WAPE computed separately for each series, then the middle value across series: how a typical single series does. Lower is better. Unit: percent. Keep in mind: Series with no actual volume have no WAPE and are left out (their number is shown). Sparse series can exceed 100%.

Classification and customer scoring
- Log loss (Log loss): How surprised the model is by what happened, using its scores as probabilities: confident wrong scores are punished hard. Lower is better. Unit: score. Keep in mind: Meaningful only if the scores behave like probabilities; probabilities are clipped to [0.000001, 0.999999]. No constant-forecast reference was recorded for it, so it cannot be read as better or worse than a baseline.
- Top-decile lift (Top-10% lift): The share of the 10% highest-scored customers who turned out inactive, divided by the share among all customers. 1.0 is no better than picking at random. Higher is better. Unit: multiple. Keep in mind: Ranking check against a proxy label (no purchase in the window), not churn. Based on a small group, so it moves a lot with few customers.
- Inactive rate in the top 10% (Top-10% rate): The share of the 10% highest-scored customers who bought nothing in the label window. For context; not a quality score. Unit: ratio. Keep in mind: Read together with the overall positive rate.
- Area under the ROC curve (ROC-AUC): How well the score ranks customers who did the event above those who did not: 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect ranking. Higher is better. Unit: score. Keep in mind: Measures ranking only. It says nothing about whether the score is a true probability.
- Area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC): How precise the top-ranked customers are across all cut-offs. More informative than ROC-AUC when the event is rare. Higher is better. Unit: score. Keep in mind: Its baseline is the event rate (prevalence), not 0.5.
- Precision (Precision): Of the customers flagged as positive, the share that really were. Higher is better. Unit: ratio. Keep in mind: Depends on the cut-off used.
- Recall (Recall): Of the customers who really were positive, the share that were flagged. Higher is better. Unit: ratio. Keep in mind: Depends on the cut-off used.
- F1 score (F1): A single number combining precision and recall (their harmonic mean). Higher is better. Unit: ratio. Keep in mind: Depends on the cut-off; ignores true negatives.
- Accuracy (Accuracy): The share of customers classified correctly, computed from the confusion matrix. Higher is better. Unit: ratio. Keep in mind: Misleading when one class is rare: predicting the majority class for everyone already scores high.
- Decision threshold (Threshold): The score above which a customer is flagged. Chosen on validation data, never on the test data. For context; not a quality score. Unit: score.

Calibration diagnostics (classification)
- Brier score of a constant forecast (Brier (constant)): The Brier score of always predicting the positive rate of the evaluated rows. A model's Brier score should be below it to add anything. For context; not a quality score. Unit: score. Keep in mind: Uses the evaluated rows' own positive rate, which makes it a demanding reference.
- Brier improvement over the constant forecast (Brier vs constant): How much lower (positive) or higher (negative) the model's Brier score is than the constant forecast's, on the same rows. Higher is better. Unit: percent. Keep in mind: Computed from two recorded Brier scores; it is not a new measurement.
- Brier score (Brier): The average squared gap between the score and what happened (0 or 1). Lower is better. Unit: score. Keep in mind: Only a true probability error if the score is calibrated; compare with the Brier score of always predicting the event rate.
- Expected calibration error (ECE): How far, on average, the score is from the observed event rate within bands of the score. Lower is better. Unit: ratio. Keep in mind: Only meaningful when the event rate in the evaluation data matches the training data.

Sample and data-quality counts
- Evaluated points (n): How many actual values the metrics were computed on. For context; not a quality score. Unit: count. Keep in mind: Small samples make every metric unstable.
- Zero-valued actuals (Zeros): How many of the evaluated actual values were exactly zero (percentage errors are undefined there). For context; not a quality score. Unit: count.
- Left-out invalid points (Invalid): Prediction/actual pairs that were missing or not finite and were left out of the metrics. For context; not a quality score. Unit: count.
- Positive rate (prevalence) (Positive rate): The share of evaluated customers for whom the event happened. For context; not a quality score. Unit: ratio. Keep in mind: Needed to read precision, PR-AUC and accuracy.
